chunks: "The convention is: ground on layer 2, ground on the layer next to the bottom, and more ground planes wherever there's an inner signal layer that needs one.
On a two-layer board it's the bottom layer.

On a four-layer board it's layer 2, directly under the top signals, with power on layer 3 and the bottom layer for more signals; sometimes layer 3 is ground too if I want both outer layers to have a ground neighbour.
On six layers it's layers 2 and 5, so each outer layer sits next to a ground and the inner signal layer sits between a ground and a power plane.
On eight and more I keep adding grounds so every signal layer is next to one.

The reasons: the outer layers are the ones with parts and the fastest, most exposed routing, and the prepreg next to them is thin, so a ground plane there gives a tight return, narrow 50 ohm traces and a small loop.
Putting ground right beside power makes a capacitor that helps decoupling. Ground in the middle shields inner signal layers from each other.
And the stack stays symmetric so it doesn't warp.
I don't normally put the planes on the outer layers because that's where the components and routing are; there I use pours stitched to the planes."
